title: ME08A: Ordinary Rhythms That Build Extraordinary Adaptability
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Using the story of a leader named Maya, Claydon argues that adaptability is a design choice rather than a personality trait. Most rigidity, he says, is structural, living in overloaded calendars and misaligned incentives, so no mindset program can fix it. His answer is ritual: small, repeatable patterns that keep a team coordinated while conditions shift, which he likens to workouts in a leadership gym. He walks through three flexibility rituals: quarterly Clarity sessions that translate strategy slogans into real bets, Coherence calls where each lead tells a six-point story, and Collaboration meetings where a junior chairs and seniors listen. The essay concludes that ordinary, boring routines beat inspirational speeches because repetition builds discipline under motion.
points: Adaptability is better treated as a structural design problem than a personality trait, since rigidity usually comes from calendars, incentives and mixed signals.
Clarity rituals work by translating corporate pillars into concrete team bets each quarter rather than repeating slogans.
Replacing slide-based updates with a six-point story from each lead turns defensive reporting into joint sensemaking.
Letting juniors run meetings surfaces hidden waste and builds psychological safety without teaching it.
Boring, repeated rituals outlast inspiration because they hold under pressure.
quotes: Most rigidity isn’t psychological — it’s structural. It lives in overloaded calendars, misaligned incentives, and strategy decks that say one thing while the system rewards another.
Maya’s insight came slowly: adaptability isn’t a personality trait or a moral virtue. It’s a design choice. Flexible teams aren’t made by inspiration.
A ritual is simply a rhythm held with intent. It might look ordinary — a meeting, a check-in, a debrief — but when designed well, it becomes a muscle memory for complexity.
Clarity, Maya learned, wasn’t repetition of slogans. It was translation. When you anchor purpose this way, the team moves in rhythm — energy spent usefully, not noisily.
Over months, these sessions replaced defensive updates with joint sensemaking. Teams stopped tripping over one another. The rhythm became smoother.
By creating a safe micro-ritual for dissent, Maya built psychological safety without needing to “teach” it. The structure did the work.
The irony is almost comic: the most effective flexibility rituals look boring. They are the part of leadership most people skip because they lack glamour — and therefore, they work.
